title: Categories of SQL Statements
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of categories of sql statements.
Apply data query language concepts in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn categories of sql statements through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Categories of SQL Statements matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of categories of sql statements is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Data Query Language concepts, Data Definition Language (DDL), Data Manipulation Language (DML), Data Control Language (DCL). Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Data Query Language concepts
items.text: Data Query Language concepts helps you choose useful data types, write readable statements, understand identifiers and literals, and recognize behavior that varies across SQL engines. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Data Definition Language (DDL)
items.text: Data Definition Language (DDL) changes how data is represented or exposed. Check dependencies, name objects consistently, keep structural changes in reviewed migrations, and rehearse the operation against a disposable copy before production.

items.title: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
items.text: Data Manipulation Language (DML) changes stored data. Preview the target rows, specify a restrictive predicate where appropriate, validate constraints, and wrap related changes in a transaction that can be reviewed before commit.

items.title: Data Control Language (DCL)
items.text: Data Control Language (DCL) helps you choose useful data types, write readable statements, understand identifiers and literals, and recognize behavior that varies across SQL engines. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Transaction Control Language (TCL)
items.text: Transaction Control Language (TCL) is about keeping multi-step work correct when errors or other sessions intervene. Keep transactions short, define what must succeed together, handle conflicts explicitly, and test using separate sessions in a disposable database.

content_blocks.code: SELECT 42::integer AS item_count, 19.95::numeric(8,2) AS unit_price, DATE '2026-01-10' AS sample_date, TRUE AS is_active;
content_blocks.expected_output: The result returns explicitly typed numeric, date, and Boolean values. The :: cast syntax is PostgreSQL-specific; CAST(value AS type) is the standard-style alternative.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable local PostgreSQL database such as codeleaf_sql_lab after loading datasets/postgresql-lab-setup.sql. Do not use production credentials or a production database. Some specialist examples require optional extensions or a specific PostgreSQL version, as stated in the lesson. The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

hints: Begin with the subtopic data query language concepts and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

summary: Categories of SQL Statements is about making the database behavior and the expected result explicit.
Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
Keep vendor-specific syntax, access assumptions, and production-safety boundaries visible.
